topic: Ransomware detection, prevention, and incident response - systematic literature review (PRISMA-style)
item: E. AI-era threat models (LLM/GenAI ransomware) - Ransomware 3.0, PromptLock, GenAI-generated polymorphic attack payloads

title.value: Unleashing offensive artificial intelligence: Automated attack technique code generation
From ChatGPT to ThreatGPT: Impact of Generative AI in Cybersecurity and Privacy

authors.value: Iturbe, E.; Llorente-Vazquez, O.; Rego, A.; Rios, E.; Toledo, N.
Gupta, M.; Akiri, C.; Aryal, K.; Parker, E.; Praharaj, L.

quartile_sjr.value: Q1 (Computers & Security, Scimago SJR 2024 = 1.445, Computer Science (miscellaneous) and Law)

study_type.value: Empirical experiment (AI-powered attack-technique generation mechanism and controlled attack simulation analysis)
Survey / threat-model analysis (perspective study with demonstrated example attacks)

methodology.value: Builds an AI-powered mechanism for the automatic generation of attack technique code, spanning initial access vectors through impact actions (including encryption and extortion-related impact), driven by Large Language Model technology; comprehensive analysis of simulated attacks identifies which MITRE-aligned attack tactics and techniques are most readily generated by LLMs; positions the mechanism as an enhancer for Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) platforms

Analyzes generative-AI (ChatGPT-class) vulnerabilities and their dual use: demonstrates jailbreak, reverse-psychology, and prompt-injection attacks that bypass model ethical constraints; examines offensive scenarios (social engineering, phishing, automated hacking, attack payload generation, malware creation, and polymorphic malware via GenAI) and defensive responses (defense automation, threat intelligence, secure code generation, malware detection, ethical guidelines, incident-response planning)

key_findings.value: Empirically demonstrates that LLM technology can be easily used for attack execution: multiple attack tactics and techniques (from initial vectors to impact actions) are consistently generated in code form; single attack techniques can be produced in multiple variants, enabling AI-enhanced attack simulation to bolster BAS-driven security assessment

Successful proof-of-concept attacks show GenAI tools can be misused by adversaries to create social-engineering content, phishing lures, attack payloads, malicious code snippets, and polymorphic malware despite OpenAI's ethical policies; the paper frames parallel defensive uses (automated threat intelligence, secure coding, incident-response plans) and enumerates open challenges for making GenAI secure, safe, trustworthy, and ethical

limitations.value: Focus is on automated generation of aircraft-/system-level attack techniques rather than a complete autonomous attack campaign; generation depends on current LLM capability and prompt engineering; evaluation is simulation-based in controlled scenarios rather than in-the-wild attestation

Conceptual threat modeling with selected proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than a systematic measurement of real attack prevalence; ransomware covered as one offensive scenario within broader GenAI misuse; technical detail is fast-dated given rapid model evolution

research_gaps.value: Identifies the gap of scalable, automated red-teaming: BAS platforms lack automatic generation of multiple, varied attack techniques; AI-generated attack variants imply defenders must test against a widened attack space rather than fixed playbooks

Highlights open challenges of both offensive and defensive GenAI: model jailbreaking and prompt injection, lack of uniform guidance for AI-assisted incident response, need for secure-by-default model deployment, and social/legal/ethical implications of GenAI misuse

inclusion_rationale.value: Peer-reviewed journal article, 2024 (within 2022-2026), Computers & Security (SJR Q1), indexed in ScienceDirect/Scopus; directly serves the item-E adversarial pillar (attacker-side AI) with LLM-generated attack techniques up to encryption/extortion-level impact actions; no eligibility criterion failed.

Peer-reviewed journal article, 2023 (within 2022-2026), IEEE Access (SJR 2023 = 0.960, Q1), indexed in IEEE Xplore; in scope for GenAI-generated polymorphic malware threat modeling; noted deviation: ransomware is treated within the broader GenAI misuse threat landscape rather than as the sole focus.

platform_environment.value: [uncertain] the paper does not fix a single target platform; attack-technique generation is evaluated conceptually across IT-system attack surfaces
[uncertain] platform-agnostic treatment of GenAI-enabled cybercrime scenarios (chatbot clients and generated code target multiple platforms)

kill_chain_stage.value: Full kill chain from initial access through post-encryption impact (covers generation of techniques mapping to encryption/extortion impact, i.e., MITRE T1485/T1471 impact stage among others)
Pre-encryption and full-chain conceptual coverage (payload generation, phishing/social engineering as delivery; malware creation through impact)

dataset_benchmark.value: [uncertain] evaluation based on simulated attack-technique scenarios; no named public ransomware benchmark dataset reported

evaluation_metrics.value: Qualitative success analysis of generated attack techniques and tactic/technique likeliness ranking; no detection metrics (attack-side study)
Qualitative demonstration of successful jailbreak/prompt-injection attacks; no quantitative detection or attack metrics reported

reproducibility.value: [uncertain] no public code or benchmark release identified at search time; simulation design is described at framework level without exhaustive prompts/configurations released in the verified record
[uncertain] demonstration prompts and jailbreak examples are described in the paper, but no artifact release (code/dataset) identified; fast model-version drift limits replication fidelity

threat_actor_fields.value: Not applicable (study models cybercriminal capability expansion in general - e.g., hacker-as-a-service - without naming a specific RaaS group)
Not applicable (no RaaS group attribution or leak-site evidence; discusses generic cyber offenders)
